awd_abstract_narration:
Pennsylvania State University will organize and host the Third Penn State SETI Symposium, from August 18-21, 2025.   This international conference will bring together a broad range of expertise to the problem of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), host a gathering of early career SETI researchers, and feature breakout sessions on specialized topics such as SETI post-detection protocols. The symposium will include theory, practice, and social aspects of the field, including radio, laser, exoplanetary, and solar system SETI.  The symposium will cater heavily towards junior scientist involvement.  The symposium will include contributions from anthropologists, historians, and others outside the physical sciences.

SETI is a broad and interdisciplinary endeavor. Thinking about how technological life will be discovered requires consideration of more than just physics or astrophysics.  Discovery might be via radio waves, or optical communication, or via atmospheric pollutants of exoplanets, via a probe in the solar system, or from the detection of the waste heat of industry in space around another star. Exploring this requires input from exoplanetary astrophysics, stellar astrophysics, planetary science, radio astronomy, electrical engineering, high energy astrophysics, and more. Technology also implies and underlying social structure, which means we must also consider how alien species might communicate, evolve, spread, and innovate.  This breadth and interdisciplinarity cannot be well represented at any typical scientific meeting; it requires a deliberate and holistic approach over multiple days, and participation by some who may not be SETI experts or even astronomers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This grant supported travel costs for researchers to attend the Third Penn State SETI Symposium, held in University Park, PA,  August 18-21, 2025.

The award sought to increase participation of a subject-matter-diverse group of researchers, especially early career researchers, in the conference.

In order to facilitate workforce and professional development in SETI, funds from this award heavily prioritized career stage: 22 (61%) of the supported researchers were early career, and 70% of the funds went towards their participant costs.

The acceptance of abstracts, speaking slots, and the award of travel funding from all sources was made without regard to demographics other than career stage

All of the funds were distributed directly to participants according to federal and Penn State travel reimbursement rules.  36 participants received partial or full support from this grant.

 

The symposium was a major opportunity for training and professional development for early career researchers. Many such researchers were given poster or plenary speaking slots, often for the first time in their careers on the topic of SETI (or at all).  A meeting of the “Order of the Octopus” at the symposium provided networking opportunities for all early career researchers in attendance.  Breakout sessions on narrower topics, including a primer on SETI, provided further education and training for all participants.

 

The impact on society from SETI, including but not limited to the impact of a successful detection, is a major aspect of SETI that was the topic of multiple talks and dedicated breakout sessions at the symposium.
